analysis.one_liner: Replaces federal income taxes with a flat 20% tax on wages and business income, repeals the estate tax.
analysis.headline: The Flat Tax Act of 2003 was introduced by one senator, drew zero cosponsors, sat in the Senate Finance Committee without ever getting a vote, and died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: Sen. Arlen Specter's bill would repeal the existing income tax and replace it with a flat 20% tax on wages and active business income. Under the design, investment income — dividends, interest, and capital gains — would not be taxed at all, and the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes would be repealed outright. The bill also repeals the financing system for retired coal miners' health benefits and the public checkoff that helps fund presidential campaigns. It never received a vote, a committee markup, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households whose money comes from investments would pay nothing on dividends, interest, or capital gains, since the new tax reaches only wages and active business income. Heirs to large estates would pay no estate or gift tax. Coal companies would be freed from the payments that finance retired miners' health benefits. High wage earners would also see their top rate fall to 20% from the mid-30s rates in effect in 2003.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, large estates, and coal companies

how_it_helps.text: The new tax reaches only 'taxable earned income' — wages, salaries, and professional fees — and the business tax applies only to 'gross active income,' which the text defines as income other than investment income. Households living on dividends, interest, and capital gains would owe no federal income tax.
The bill repeals the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes entirely for deaths and transfers after December 31, 2003, eliminating the tax on very large inheritances.

Businesses would pay a flat 20% on active business income after deducting inputs, employee compensation, and equipment costs — a top corporate-style rate well below the 35% statutory corporate rate in effect in 2003, with no tax on investment returns.
The bill repeals the subtitle of the tax code that finances coal industry health benefits, ending the payments coal operators make under that system.
It also repeals the public financing provisions for presidential elections, including the income tax checkoff that funds them.

analysis.who_pays: Wage earners would bear the load: every dollar of wages above a family's deductions would be taxed at a flat 20%, and the replacement system allows only a standard deduction, a capped $2,500 cash charitable deduction, and a home-mortgage interest deduction — the credits and deductions of the current code would not carry over. Because capital income would go entirely untaxed while wages are taxed, the tax burden shifts from people who own assets toward people who work for a paycheck. Retired coal miners would lose the financing system behind their health benefits, and the revenue lost from repealing the income, estate, and gift taxes would have to be made up somewhere — through higher rates on wages, cuts to spending, or federal borrowing.
analysis.who_pays_short: Middle-class wage earners and retired coal miners

drawbacks.text: The design taxes only wages and active business income and leaves investment income untaxed, so two households with the same total income could pay vastly different taxes: a nurse earning $80,000 in wages would pay roughly $11,000 after deductions, while someone with $80,000 in dividends and capital gains would pay nothing.

The replacement system allows only a standard deduction, a cash charitable deduction capped at $2,500, and a home-mortgage interest deduction. Nothing in the new scheme preserves the child tax credit or the earned income credit, so the bill's own CRS summary lists no family credits at all in the replacement tax.
Repealing the coal industry health benefits subtitle would end the statutory financing for retired coal miners' lifetime health coverage, leaving those benefits without a funding source.
The bill repeals the public financing of presidential elections and its tax checkoff, leaving presidential campaigns reliant entirely on private money.

A complete repeal of the income, estate, and gift taxes replaced by a 20% flat rate would raise far less from those at the top, since top rates in 2003 ran in the mid-to-high 30s and capital gains, dividends, and estates would face zero tax — a gap that means higher taxes on wages, program cuts, or borrowing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are concentrated almost entirely at the top: investment income goes untaxed, the estate tax disappears, and coal companies stop paying for retiree health coverage. The costs land on people who earn wages — a flat 20% on every dollar above modest deductions with none of the current code's family credits — and on retired coal miners, whose health benefits lose their funding. A flat-tax advocate would point to the $27,500 standard deduction for a family of four and simpler filing, but the core arithmetic of the bill is a transfer from wage income to capital income, and its ancillary repeals (coal miner health financing, public campaign financing) compound that direction. The drawbacks are not incidental; they are the point of the design.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no markup, no vote, and no cosponsors until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Arlen Specter introduced the Flat Tax Act of 2003 in the Senate on April 11, 2003.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee; the action history shows no markup, no hearing, and no floor action ever followed.
Not a single senator cosponsored the bill, leaving Specter as its only supporter in the chamber.
The 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, and the bill died in committee without ever reaching the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nobody gained anything from the bill itself, but wage earners and retired coal miners were better off because it died: the shift of taxes onto wages and the repeal of coal miners' health-benefit financing never happened.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wage earners and retired coal miners

for.name: Sen. Arlen Specter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Flat Tax Act of 2003 and referred it to the Finance Committee; found no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Chair Chuck Grassley)
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred; never scheduled a markup or vote
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it never left the committee.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever recorded, and the bill's lone Republican sponsor attracted zero cosponsors from either party, so its partisan shape was never tested.

industries.note: The bill repeals the tax-code subtitle that finances coal industry health benefits, ending the payments coal operators make into that system. The saving to the industry would come directly out of retired miners' health coverage.

The bill taxes only wages and active business income, so dividends, interest, and capital gains would go untaxed, and the estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes are repealed outright. The entire burden of the new code falls on wages.
The charitable deduction would be limited to $2,500 in cash contributions per year, sharply reducing the incentive for large donors to give compared with current law's unlimited deduction.
